subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of variation caused mostly by the environment?
questions.explain: A scar is an environmental (acquired) variation, not caused by genes.

questions.q: Identical twins have the same genes but can still show small differences. These differences are caused by:
questions.explain: Identical twins share the same genotype, so any differences between them are due to environmental factors.

questions.q: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA are a problem because:
options: Existing antibiotics no longer kill them, so infections are hard to treat
They are killed instantly by all antibiotics
They reproduce too slowly to spread
questions.explain: Resistant bacteria survive treatment, making infections difficult to cure and able to spread between people.

questions.q: A farmer breeds the cows that produce the most milk together over many generations. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Choosing parents with a desired trait (high milk yield) to breed together over generations is selective breeding.

questions.q: Meiosis produces:
questions.explain: Meiosis produces four non-identical haploid gametes, each with half the normal number of chromosomes.

questions.q: How many pairs of chromosomes are found in a normal human body cell?
questions.explain: Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total), one of each pair from each parent.

questions.q: A pea plant for tallness has the genotype Tt. Its phenotype will be:
options: Short, because it has a t allele
questions.explain: T is dominant, so a Tt (heterozygous) plant shows the dominant tall phenotype.

questions.q: A homozygous dominant parent (BB) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (bb). What proportion of offspring will show the recessive phenotype?
questions.explain: All offspring are Bb (heterozygous), so they all show the dominant phenotype and none show the recessive one.

questions.q: Selective breeding (artificial selection) involves:
options: Letting nature choose which organisms survive
Humans choosing organisms with desired traits to breed together
questions.explain: In selective breeding humans choose parents with desirable characteristics to breed over many generations.

questions.q: Studying the genome (DNA) of organisms has improved classification because it:
options: Replaces the need for naming organisms
Proves that all species are identical
Shows how closely related species are by comparing their DNA
questions.explain: Comparing DNA reveals evolutionary relationships, leading to changes such as the three-domain classification system.

questions.q: Which of these is a key part of natural selection?
options: Individuals with advantageous variations are more likely to survive and reproduce
Organisms choosing to change to suit their environment
Characteristics changing only within one lifetime
All organisms in a species being identical
questions.explain: In natural selection, individuals with advantageous inherited variations survive, reproduce and pass on those alleles.

questions.q: Two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) are crossed. What is the expected ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes in the offspring?
questions.explain: A Bb × Bb cross gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes (BB, Bb, Bb, bb).

questions.q: What determines whether a human baby is biologically male or female?
options: Whether the sperm carries an X or Y chromosome
Whether the egg carries an X or Y chromosome
questions.explain: Eggs always carry X; the sperm carries either X (giving XX, female) or Y (giving XY, male), so the sperm determines sex.

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) are crossed. What is the chance of a child having the disorder?
questions.explain: Two carriers (Ff × Ff) have a 1 in 4 chance of producing an affected ff child.

questions.q: Why did it take a long time for Darwin's theory to be widely accepted?
options: It conflicted with religious beliefs and the mechanism of inheritance was not yet known
No one was interested in biology
questions.explain: Darwin's theory challenged religious views and lacked a known mechanism of inheritance (genes were not yet understood).

questions.q: What is the genome of an organism?
options: The entire genetic material of that organism
questions.explain: The genome is the entire genetic material (all the DNA) of an organism.

questions.q: Which of these provides direct evidence for evolution?
options: Fossils showing how organisms have changed over time
questions.explain: Fossils show how species have gradually changed over millions of years, providing evidence for evolution.

questions.q: How does meiosis differ from mitosis?
options: Mitosis makes gametes; meiosis makes body cells
Meiosis halves the chromosome number and makes varied gametes; mitosis makes identical diploid cells
questions.explain: Meiosis halves chromosome number to form varied gametes, whereas mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the difference between selective breeding and genetic engineering?
options: Selective breeding transfers genes; genetic engineering chooses parents
They are exactly the same process
Both involve changing genes with enzymes only
Selective breeding chooses which organisms breed; genetic engineering transfers genes directly between organisms
questions.explain: Selective breeding selects breeding pairs over generations, while genetic engineering directly moves a gene into an organism.

questions.q: A heterozygous brown-eyed parent (Bb) and a blue-eyed parent (bb) have children, where brown (B) is dominant. What ratio of brown to blue eyes is expected?
questions.explain: A Bb x bb cross gives Bb and bb offspring in equal numbers, a 1:1 ratio of brown to blue eyes.

questions.q: A herd of giraffes lives where food is high in the trees. Over many generations, longer necks become common. The best explanation is that:
options: All giraffes decided to grow longer necks
Giraffes with longer necks survived better and reproduced, passing on the alleles
Giraffes stretched their necks and passed this on
The trees caused the necks to grow
questions.explain: Natural selection: giraffes with naturally longer necks reached more food, survived and passed on those alleles.

questions.q: Which is a real example of genetic engineering?
options: Dogs bred for a calm temperament
Bacteria modified to produce human insulin
questions.explain: Bacteria can be genetically modified to make human insulin, used to treat diabetes.
